screenings.title: Detour
screenings.description: Hearing a certain tune spin on the jukebox in an all-night diner in Reno sends down-on-his-luck pianist Al Roberts (Tom Neal) on a traumatic trip down memory lane, recalling his fateful roadside encounter with Ann Savage’s aptly named femme fatale Vera and his subsequent subjugation to her, in Ulmer’s made-for-peanuts classic of noir absurdism, one of the priceless treasures to emerge from Hollywood’s so-called “Poverty Row” studios. “Possibly the bleakest, most doom-laden film noir ever… Savage’s sensational performance, combined with the real-life trajectory of Neal, who ended up going to prison for murdering his wife, have made this a tormented film with the despairing logic of nightmare.” —The Los Angeles Times

screenings.title: Two Seasons, Two Strangers preceded by Nagahama
screenings.description: Based on two manga by Yoshiharu Tsuge, who rose to underground celebrity thanks to his surrealist tales published in the pages of Garo, the bastion of Japanese avant-garde cartooning, Miyake’s bifurcated live-action feature observes (and draws parallels and contrasts from) a summertime meet-cute between Nagisa and Natsuo (Yuumi Kawai and Mansaku Takada) and a snowbound winter encounter between screenwriter Li and innkeeper Ben-zō (Shim Eun-kyung and Shinichi Tsutsumi). Winner of the Golden Leopard at last year’s Locarno Film Festival, hailed “a true masterpiece” by Shiguéhiko Hasumi, Japan’s greatest living film critic, Two Seasons, Two Strangers is at one and the same time as simple as its straightforward title suggests and immensely, exhilaratingly complex. Preceded by Miyake’s short Nagahama, born of a creative collaboration with dancer and actress Shizuka Ishibashi.

screenings.title: Sloan Showcase: After Yang with Kogonada in person + Verse
screenings.description: EMBODIED TECHNOLOGY With directors Kogonada and Noam Argov in person After Yang. Dir. Kogonada. 2022, 96 mins. With Colin Farrell, Justin H. Min, Jodie Turner-Smith, Haley Lu Richardson, Malea Emma Tjandrawidjaja. When his young daughter’s technosapien companion, the android Yang (Min), malfunctions, Jake (Farrell) must come to terms with what this loss means for his family. Adapted from a short story by Alexander Weinstein, and directed with aesthetic precision and restraint by Kogonada, the director of tender films about interpersonal connection such as Columbus and this year’s Zi, After Yang is a sensitive and visually striking inquiry into what it means to be human. Preceded by Verse. Dir. Noam Argov. 2026, 18 mins. With Taj Cross, Jesse LaTourette, Will Dagger. Seventeen-year-old Adam is forced to confront where his virtual persona ends and his physical self begins when he decides to meet his VR girlfriend in real life. Both of these films have received recognition and/or support from the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation’s program in Public Understanding of Science and Technology. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / free for MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission. Visitors are encouraged to view the exhibition Overexposed: Art, Technology, and the Body, which can be added on to their film ticket for $2.50. Special Guests: Kogonada is a writer and director. His first feature, Columbus, premiered at the Sundance Film Festival in 2017. Noam Argov is an award-winning writer/director and National Geographic Explorer whose work explores identity and the spaces between worlds. Her 2023 narrative short Sulam (Ladder) premiered in competition at Aspen Shortsfest and won Best U.S. Student Film at Palm Springs ShortFest; her feature screenplay Princess won NYU’s Purple List Table-Read Initiative, where it was staged in its entirety for producers and executives; and her latest short, Verse, received the Sloan Production Award for its exploration of VR and neuroscience and had its world premiere at the 2026 Tribeca Film Festival. Noam is also a producer on Forbidden Fruits (SXSW 2026), starring Lili Reinhart and Lola Tung and released theatrically by IFC, and Punter, a proof-of-concept film executive produced by Spike Lee and a finalist for the Student BAFTA. Sappir Argov is an American actor and writer whose work spans film, podcasting, and live performance. She is a co-writer of Verse. Sappir starred in short films for top-tier MFA programs, including NYU Tisch and UCLA, as well as an independent short screened for producers at Blumhouse. She is also starring in two upcoming projects slated for release in 2026. Her commercial work includes a global travel campaign aired on NBC. In her writing, Sappir’s original podcast Passing Through ranked in the Top 100 narrative comedy shows on Apple Podcasts.

screenings.title: Personal Problems | The Ravishing Cinema of Bill Gunn
screenings.description: What happens when a group of unbankable individuals tell their stories? Actors who have final say over their speaking parts? A director who was found ‘too difficult’ for Hollywood? A composer who would not submit the hack soundtracks required by the industry? A Black male lead who was not Black enough? A Black actress who was not light enough? An actor who had been retired because he belonged to another era? A cinematographer who chose art over expediency? An unmarketable co-actor who didn’t look like Clark Gable or a male version of Vanessa Williams? Two producers, having no experience, had the audacity to organize a production with the amount of money that Hollywood spends on catering? Maybe less.

screenings.title: After Winter Comes Spring
screenings.description: "Shot in luminous black-and-white, Misselwitz’s After Winter Comes Spring travels a German Democratic Republic that very soon will be no more, conversing with women of all ages on stops along the way to create a group portrait of female East Germany—one that interrogates the outgoing leadership’s claims of advancing equality between the genders while looking anxiously towards the new world in the process of being born. “‘At the age of 40 I set out once again from the town of my childhood,’ explains Misselwitz at the start of her railway journey, ‘to discover how others have lived and how they want to live.’ Her film exists in the gap between the two. The women she meets speak plainly of regret, longing, and hope: the teenage runaways, the divorcée split between factory work and caring for her disabled daughter, and the great-grandmother who, after 60 years of marriage, quietly admits it was a mistake to marry her husband.” —Series curator Genevieve Yue"

screenings.title: White Snail
screenings.description: NEW YORK PREMIERE! FILMMAKERS IN PERSON!“Following two unconventional documentaries – SPACE DOGS (2019) and DREAMING DOGS (2024) – focused on the lives of stray canines, filmmaking duo Elsa Kremser and Levin Peter return with the narrative feature WHITE SNAIL, where the two protagonists also exhibit a fondness for various animals. Set in contemporary Belarus, the film tells the story of Masha, a blonde, thin, fair-skinned model pursuing her dream job in China, and Misha, a tattooed, thickset painter working at a morgue. Played with extreme naturalness by non-professionals Marya Imbro and Mikhail Senkov, these two loners strike up an unlikely but profound friendship that will force them to confront their secrets and wounds. The worlds to which Masha and Misha belong are completely at odds. But as these characters form a strange bond, the fashion industry and the funeral business reveal equally unlikely coincidences and areas of overlap that subtly proliferate as the plot advances. By depicting how we and our bodies relate to sight and touch, life and death, reality and imagination, flaws and perfection, Kremser and Peter map two universes on to one another, leaving the viewer to determine where they intersect and whether they diverge.” –Cristina Álvarez López, VIENNALEThese screenings are co-presented by Deutsches Haus at NYU and Erste Bank, on the occasion of the co-awarding of the 2025 Viennale Erste Bank Film Award to WHITE SNAIL. Since 2011, each annual edition of the Viennale (Vienna International FilmFestival) has featured the granting of the Viennale Erste Bank Film Award to one or more filmmakers whose films are included within the festival. Designed to showcase the best of Austrian cinema, the Award was founded by Erste Bank, the Viennale’s main sponsor, and is awarded according to the findings of an independent jury. The Award brings a cash prize as well as a residency as a visiting filmmaker organized by Deutsches Haus at NYU. Additional support for these screenings has been provided by the Austrian Cultural Forum New York.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Asako I & II
screenings.description: Following up Happy Hour, his justly acclaimed epic of everyday life, Hamaguchi offers a different but no less quietly revolutionary vision with this pop romance that moves from youthful exuberance and delusion to mature circumspection and compromise, while keeping up throughout a magical tonal balance of wistfulness, comic buoyancy, and the ineffably heartbreaking. As a student in Osaka, Asako meets and falls in love with a drifter named Baku who one day drifts right out of her life. Two years later, working in Tokyo, she sees Baku again—or, rather, a young, solid businessman named Ryohei who is Baku’s double in every respect save personality. After initial astonishment, they begin to build a life together—but a twist in circumstances threatens to tear it all down, and forces Asako to confront her long, lingering love affair with a half-ghost fantasy.

screenings.title: The Woman in the Window
screenings.description: Alone for the holiday while his wife and children are on vacation, the staid, middle-aged college professor Richard Wanley (Edward G. Robinson) is about to settle in to an uneventful stretch of nights spent sipping port by the fireplace of his club—but then he catches a glimpse of a beguiling brunette in a gallery window and, in short order, finds himself having a drink with the model (Joan Bennett), after which everything goes straight to hell. Involved in a self-defense killing and its subsequent cover-up, Wanley finds himself investigating his own crime at the elbow of fellow clubman and D.A. Frank Lalor (Raymond Massey), the noose tightening around his neck with the emergence of every fresh clue and misstep. A high-style turning-of-the-screws noir suspenser, with a wonderfully oleaginous turn from heel extraordinaire Dan Duryea.

screenings.description: Argento’s return to his giallo roots after veering off into gonzo horror/fantasy, Tenebrae features Anthony Franciosa as an American author of potboiler thrillers who, promoting a new book in Rome, finds that a murderer is re-enacting his most ghoulish delights of literary fancy. Argento uses the occasion to scale new, dizzying heights of his own, employing bravura crane shots, brazenly baroque lighting, and the iconic moment of a razor slashing through white cotton.

screenings.title: The Brood
screenings.description: In The Brood, the bitter divorce between the mentally disturbed Nola (Samantha Eggar) and her ex-husband Frank (Art Hindle) was pretty messy, so it should be a good sign that she’s finally getting professional help from the renowned Dr. Hal Raglan (Oliver Reed)—but Frank can’t help but notice that people on Nola’s long list of enemies keep dying at the hands of asexual, dwarfish assassins, and so he starts to wonder what exactly the experimental therapy practiced at Dr. Raglan’s Somafree Institute consists of… Written while Cronenberg was in the midst of his own divorce and custody battle, The Brood is a brutal, bracing airing of anxieties gussied up in grindhouse trappings.

screenings.title: Spellbound
screenings.description: Hitchcock goes in for psychoanalysis in this singular thriller, made under the influence of Sigmund Freud and Salvador Dalí, the latter of whom designed the dazzling dream sequence. Analyst Ingrid Bergman falls for amnesiac patient Gregory Peck—but is there a murderer’s heart lurking beneath that dapper exterior? The delirium only grows more intense and Miklós Rózsa’s theremin-inflected score becomes more urgent as her doubts grow and she draws closer to the truth.

screenings.title: The General
screenings.description: Keaton’s engineer Johnnie Gray is another of his big-hearted little guys, rejected by the Confederate Army, though when the Union tries to make off with his train, runt Johnnie shows his mettle in the most incredible sustained chase sequence in all of silent comedy. Wall-to-wall with elaborate, antic gags, though also marked by a quiet sense of pastoral beauty that had previously been given little outlet.

screenings.title: The Killing
screenings.description: Dir. Stanley Kubrick. 1956. 85 mins. 35mm. With Sterling Hayden, Coleen Gray, Vince Edwards, Jay C. Flippen, Elisha Cook Jr., Marie Windsor. Stanley Kubrick and pulp-fiction legend Jim Thompson co-wrote this darkly comic thriller about a racetrack heist gone awry. With its thick layers of irony and stopwatch-precise playing with time, Kubrick’s fragmented crime noir (whose existential overtones and intricate structure inspired Quentin Tarantino’s Reservoir Dogs) is his true narrative breakthrough, laying the groundwork for a filmography of flawed, failed masculinity and fatalistic humor. screenings.title: Fireflies Press presents Hermia & Helena
screenings.description: Camila (Agustina Muñoz), a young Argentine theater director, travels from Buenos Aires to New York for an artistic residency where she intends to develop her new project: a new Spanish translation of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream—but upon her arrival, Camila quickly realizes that her work isn’t compensating for the loss of her friends and boyfriend she left behind. A film of quiet passion in which small gestures and objects carry great emotional weight, Hermia & Helena was the first film Piñeiro made in his adoptive home of New York City, released 10 years ago, and as such is ideally suited to screen alongside the stateside launch of his new artist’s book from Fireflies Press, From where do you start when drawing a flower?

screenings.title: The Battle of Tuntenhaus
screenings.description: Juliet BashoreTHE BATTLE OF TUNTENHAUS, PART 1 1991, 24 min, DCP. In German with English subtitles.THE BATTLE OF TUNTENHAUS, PART 2 1992, 19 min, DCP. In German with English subtitles.“The Wall has fallen. Berlin has reunified. But there are new zones of transgression to be carved out and explored. Mainzer Straße is a hot spot of squatters and anti-fascist fights. One of the squats on this notorious street, the Tuntenhaus (‘House of Queers’), becomes a specific target of both their neo-Nazi neighbors and the iron fist of the capitalist state. Juliet Bashore’s legendary documentary follows the daily struggle of the queens and queers to create and defend a place for themselves in the chaos and unrest after the fall of communism. The extraordinary union of the anarchist/autonomous and gay scenes meets the onlooking yet involved sympathizers, who also end up in conflict with the squatters as a result of their filming. The film is a unique testimony to the violent and momentous eviction of the people from the streets.” –THE BEACONCLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Suzhou River
screenings.description: Taking its name from the polluted river that flows through Shanghai, director Lou’s hometown, the brooding Suzhou River uses the singular first-person perspective of its unseen videographer-narrator to explore the grubby underbelly of the city, observing the story of an unsuspecting motorcycle courier who finds himself snared in a kidnapping plot and murder rap. A seductive, intricately structured stylistic coup from the Sixth Generation filmmaker, drawing on influences from film noir to Vertigo (1958) while developing its own idiosyncratic and haunting visual vocabulary.

screenings.title: Columbus
screenings.description: Modern architecture acts as a vehicle for emotional expression in Kogonada’s lauded first feature, whose title refers to the Indiana city that, thanks to the patronage of Cummins diesel engines company cofounder J. Irwin Miller, has commissioned buildings from master builders including I.M. Pei, Eero Saarinen, and Robert Venturi. A Korean American translator (John Cho) arrives in this curious testing ground for advanced architecture after his estranged scholar father falls ill, there to cross paths with dad’s protégée (Parker Posey), an aesthete clerk at the local library (Haley Lu Richardson), and a bevy of singular structures. A film of rich colors and muted yearning, and one of the most distinctive debuts in the last decade of American independent cinema.

The Gorgon
screenings.description: In their tireless search for new monsters to add to their menagerie Hammer turned here to Greek mythology, unleashing the fatal gaze of the Gorgon on the residents of a German village, c. 1910. Seven Vandorf residents have in recent years been found frozen into statuary, and it falls on the esteemed Prof. Meister of Leipzig (Christopher Lee) to overcome interference by local physician Dr. Namaroff (Peter Cushing) and track down the culprit, Megaera (ballerina-turned-film actor Prudence Hyman), a she-devil with the ability to turn flesh to stone. A small miracle of high style on a pinched budget, praised by Raymond Durgnat in Films and Filming for its “romantic warmth… with oil lamps casting a rich glow on the patchwork counterpanes and through coloured windows, and with some extraordinarily beautiful cloudscapes and dusk skies.”

screenings.title: zi
screenings.description: “Poetic, political, and above all incontrovertibly material” [The New Yorker], Kogonada’s fourth feature, the experimental drama zi, follows the title character, played by Michelle Mao, a concert violinist whose aimless peregrinations through the streets of Hong Kong are interrupted by visions of what may be either her past or future, a condition she attempts to explain to a new American acquaintance (Haley Lu Richardson, Columbus) while a stranger (Jin Ha) observes the pair from a distance. A valentine to the textures and colors of the Fragrant Harbor as seen by night, featuring music by the late Ryuichi Sakamoto, the formally audacious, shot-on-the-fly zi is a film of unusual delicacy and reserve, one whose air of mystery abides long after the credits have rolled.

screenings.title: Crystal Voyager
screenings.description: Directed by Elfick, co-founder of the Australian surf magazine Tracks, “the Citizen Kane of surfing pictures” [The Guardian] follows photographer, filmmaker, and avid surfer George Greenough, as well as fellow wave-chasers Nat Young and Richie West, on a quest for secluded surf spots that goes from coastal California to Lennox Head, New South Wales, to points even further afield. A heady paean to the elements, to sun and water, whose fisheye tube-riding POV shots were received as nothing short of revolutionary when it premiered, and whose psychedelic soundtrack by The Crystal Voyager Band won it an ardent following in counterculture hot spots the world over.

screenings.title: Tripolar the Movie + Q&A
screenings.description: TRIPOLAR THE MOVIE is a biting satire disguised as a stoner comedy set in the heart of Brooklyn. Rife with John Waters-style humor, the story follows a washed-up 50-something mother and her daughter’s 20-something friends who are willing to do anything to make a film. But when a movie exec greenlights their project, they begin to conspire against one another in a parody of life in modern America.

screenings.title: White Snail
screenings.description: NEW YORK PREMIERE! FILMMAKERS IN PERSON!“Following two unconventional documentaries – SPACE DOGS (2019) and DREAMING DOGS (2024) – focused on the lives of stray canines, filmmaking duo Elsa Kremser and Levin Peter return with the narrative feature WHITE SNAIL, where the two protagonists also exhibit a fondness for various animals. Set in contemporary Belarus, the film tells the story of Masha, a blonde, thin, fair-skinned model pursuing her dream job in China, and Misha, a tattooed, thickset painter working at a morgue. Played with extreme naturalness by non-professionals Marya Imbro and Mikhail Senkov, these two loners strike up an unlikely but profound friendship that will force them to confront their secrets and wounds. The worlds to which Masha and Misha belong are completely at odds. But as these characters form a strange bond, the fashion industry and the funeral business reveal equally unlikely coincidences and areas of overlap that subtly proliferate as the plot advances. By depicting how we and our bodies relate to sight and touch, life and death, reality and imagination, flaws and perfection, Kremser and Peter map two universes on to one another, leaving the viewer to determine where they intersect and whether they diverge.” –Cristina Álvarez López, VIENNALEThese screenings are co-presented by Deutsches Haus at NYU and Erste Bank, on the occasion of the co-awarding of the 2025 Viennale Erste Bank Film Award to WHITE SNAIL. Since 2011, each annual edition of the Viennale (Vienna International FilmFestival) has featured the granting of the Viennale Erste Bank Film Award to one or more filmmakers whose films are included within the festival. Designed to showcase the best of Austrian cinema, the Award was founded by Erste Bank, the Viennale’s main sponsor, and is awarded according to the findings of an independent jury. The Award brings a cash prize as well as a residency as a visiting filmmaker organized by Deutsches Haus at NYU. screenings.title: Nina Hagen = Punk + Glory
screenings.description: Up until his untimely death earlier this year, filmmaker Peter Sempel had a long and close association with Anthology Film Archives and Jonas Mekas (about whom he made four separate feature-length film portraits over the years). In addition to his collaborations with Jonas, Sempel made numerous other experimental films and documentaries about various artists and musicians. Among his best-known works is this film about the legendary singer, songwriter, and actress Nina Hagen. Far from a conventional artist doc, NINA HAGEN = PUNK + GLORY favors spontaneous, fragmentary, and often home-movie-like glimpses of her daily life, performances, and interactions with family, friends, and colleagues (including Lemmy, George Clinton, Blixa Bargeld, Udo Kier, Dee Dee Ramone, Jonas Mekas, and others). Sempel’s goal is less to narrate Hagen’s biography than to capture her unique energy and charisma, and to shed light on her many sides, on- and off-stage.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Sad Vacation
screenings.description: The third and final film of Aoyama’s “Kitakyushu Saga,” adapted from his own novel, stars Tadanobu Asano as Kenji, a young man still nursing the wounds of an unhappy childhood as he goes through the desultory motions of various odd jobs, who catches sight of an opportunity for closure—or, perhaps, revenge—when one night he recognizes the wife of one of his employers as the mother who’d abandoned him years ago, and conspires to infiltrate their household. A rich, moving human drama of families arbitrarily assigned and chosen, its large ensemble cast handled adroitly, and the proceedings given a striking, somber beauty by prodigiously gifted cinematographer Masaki Tamura.

screenings.title: Lost Highway
screenings.description: Few filmmakers have shown themselves so adept at plumbing the depths of the subconscious without coming up for air as Lynch, whose Lost Highway—inspired loosely by still-fresh coverage of the O. J. Simpson trial—begins as a dark domestic drama concerning a sexually incompetent saxophonist (Bill Pullman) and his wife (Patricia Arquette), morphs into a movie about a cocksman mechanic (Balthazar Getty) who gets involved with a gangster’s girl (Arquette, again), and ends with an unleashing of apocalyptic, purgative flame… Whether you take it as a cinematic depiction of a psychogenic fugue state or a free-associative disgorging of images from Hollywood’s id, Lynch’s film has the pull of a whirlpool and the terrible logic of a nightmare.

screenings.title: Leave Her to Heaven
screenings.description: A chilling film noir like no other, Gene Tierney stars as Ellen Berent, a beautiful and possessive woman whose overly dependent love for her husband turns increasingly sinister. Shot in gorgeous technicolor by director John M. Stahl and DP Leon Shamroy (winner of the Academy Award for Best Color Cinematography), Leave Her to Heaven became 20th Century Fox’s highest-grossing film of the 1940’s. At the rotten center is an Oscar-nominated performance from Tierney, playing the rare femme fatale who isn’t motivated by all-American greed and ambition, but instead is consumed by obsession, jealousy, and deadly devotion.

screenings.title: The Battle of Tuntenhaus
screenings.description: Juliet BashoreTHE BATTLE OF TUNTENHAUS, PART 1 1991, 24 min, DCP. In German with English subtitles.THE BATTLE OF TUNTENHAUS, PART 2 1992, 19 min, DCP. In German with English subtitles.“The Wall has fallen. Berlin has reunified. But there are new zones of transgression to be carved out and explored. Mainzer Straße is a hot spot of squatters and anti-fascist fights. One of the squats on this notorious street, the Tuntenhaus (‘House of Queers’), becomes a specific target of both their neo-Nazi neighbors and the iron fist of the capitalist state. Juliet Bashore’s legendary documentary follows the daily struggle of the queens and queers to create and defend a place for themselves in the chaos and unrest after the fall of communism. The extraordinary union of the anarchist/autonomous and gay scenes meets the onlooking yet involved sympathizers, who also end up in conflict with the squatters as a result of their filming. The film is a unique testimony to the violent and momentous eviction of the people from the streets.” –THE BEACONCLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Bitter Christmas
screenings.description: BITTER CHRISTMAS tells two alternating stories, one starring Elsa, an advertising director, in 2004, during a long weekend in December. The second takes place in 2026 and stars Raúl, a screenwriter and director who is writing a script that we soon discover is the story of Elsa, her boyfriend Bonifacio, and her friends Patricia and Natalia. Mixed with fiction, Elsa is, in a way, Raúl's alter ego, who, like him, resorts to autofiction as a solution to a long period of creative drought. He looks inside himself, and he can't help but also look at the people who make up his most intimate universe: his partner and his assistant. The film narrates the close relationship between reality and fiction, between inspiration and life, exploring the limits of autofiction and stories within stories.

screenings.title: Postcolonial Motion: Taxis and Travelogues
screenings.description: While not as long-standing as the romance with trains, cinema has a love affair with taxis. A cab ride is often more than just a means of getting from one place to another. The taxi is a cinematic apparatus in motion, a confessional, an urban microcosm, a transition, a temporary intimacy, an archive of daily life, a nightmare of forced conversation, an eavesdropper’s dream. Yet beneath such metaphors are material threats: the gig economy, prior and enduring precarities and exploitation of labor, movements of migration conditioned by colonization.POSTCOLONIAL MOTION: TAXIS AND TRAVELOGUES draws together three films combining oral testimonies and the kinetics of transport. Frank Sweeney, Karimah Ashadu, and Timoteus Anggawan Kusno each consider the movements of people, goods and images, tracing how workers warp the barriers of historical categories and economic constraints as they cross borders.Guest-programmed by Yasmina Price, who wrote the introduction and individual film descriptions.Frank SweeneyGO YE AFAR2026, 24 min, DCPIrish research-based artist Frank Sweeney’s latest work, GO YE AFAR (2026), stages a historical examination of economy, religion, national identity, and state power through the nocturnal taxi journey of a Nigerian driver in Dublin and Calabar. Making a link between the IMF’s role in imposing a debt structure on Ireland in the 2010s and the economic dependency still inflicted on the African continent, Sweeney makes a taxi journey an illuminating lens onto the dubious legacies of Catholic missionaries and European philanthropy, global privatization and the erosion of the commons.Karimah AshaduBROWN GOODS2020, 12 min, DCPBROWN GOODS (2020), by British-born Nigerian artist and director Karimah Ashadu, both shares and reconfigures a similar terrain. The film scans the intermingled economies and geographies of Africa and Europe, conjuring Nigeria from its viewpoint in Germany. The setting is specifically Hamburg, a hub of international trade and multinational corporations. Ashadu’s agile camerawork delves through docks, weaving amongst ship containers and stacks of tires as Emeka – the self-sufficient central figure, excluded from formal work due to his humanitarian status – voices a sharp analysis of manufacturing and industrial monopolies, the politics of resources and global capital.Timoteus Anggawan KusnoOBSCURA2026, 14 min, DCPIndonesian filmmaker and visual artist Timoteus Anggawan Kusno’s OBSCURA (2026) echoes the unsettling, spectral dreaminess and mediatized archival memory of GO YE AFAR. Operating between Indonesia and the Netherlands, the film critically reworks the form of the ethnographic travelogue and colonial imagery through a story of theft (another kind of informal job). Gallery workers liberate a painting and carry it out in a truck, performing how images physically travel, are taken apart, literally unframed and reframed.Total running time: ca. 55 min.The screening will be followed by a conversation with filmmaker and artist Frank Sweeney!CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Narrow Rooms: Drunken Noodles
screenings.description: Lucio CastroDRUNKEN NOODLES2025, 83 min, DCP. In English and Spanish with English subtitles.When Adnan (Laith Khalifeh) arrives in New York to work at a Lower East Side gallery for the summer, he’s newly single and ready to mingle. He cruises strangers in the park at night and begins a flirtation with a delivery driver. At work, he’s helping to exhibit the recently discovered work of Sal Salandra, a real-world gay artist and elder who crafts tableaus of gay orgies and sex club scenes in vibrant needlepoint. These artworks – and Sal himself, played by Ezriel Kornel – become the connective thread for a time-jumping narrative that unfolds in four parts. Made for little money, with a small crew and total creative control, the latest by Lucio Castro (END OF THE CENTURY) is a delightful, sexually-charged short-story collection with whimsical elements of dreamy magical realism. screenings.title: Barbara
screenings.description: With Jeanne Balibar, Mathieu Amalric, Vincent Peirani, Aurore Clement, and Grégoire Colin.Amalric’s seventh feature-length film as a director is both a heartfelt tribute to the legendary chanteuse Barbara (1930-97), and a vehicle for another peerlessly talented French luminary, the actress and singer Jeanne Balibar. Amalric’s films are remarkable for their intuitive freedom, and their emphasis on emotional textures and states of feeling rather than on straightforward narrative construction or easily grasped meanings. BARBARA is a case in point: eschewing anything like a coherent, birth-to-death account of the events of her life, the film instead orchestrates fragments of the singer’s life and performances into a free and quasi-abstract meditation on Barbara’s identity and cultural presence. And by casting Balibar not as Barbara per se but more self-referentially as an actress making a film-within-the-film about the singer, his film becomes an even broader investigation into the concept of biographical filmmaking, representation, and identity. An experimental biopic in the tradition of Stanley Kwan’s CENTER STAGE, Peter Watkins’s EDVARD MUNCH, and Paul Leduc’s FRIDA, it features a typically riveting, charismatic performance from Balibar.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Cabaret
screenings.description: Dir. Bob Fosse. 1972, 124 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Liza Minnelli, Michael York, Helmut Griem, Joel Grey, Maria Berenson. Fosse rightly won the Best Director Oscar for his shattering musical set in Berlin on the eve of Hitler’s rise to power. Liza Minnelli and Joel Grey also scored Oscars for their unforgettable performances as, respectively, Sally Bowles, a vivacious but damaged American singer selling her soul in a seedy nightclub, and the devilish emcee who presides over it. A devastating, delirious movie experience, featuring John Kander and Fred Ebb’s rousing show tunes and Geoffrey Unsworth’s gloriously ragged photography, Cabaret reinvented the movie musical for 1970s American cinema and all but wrote a new cinematic grammar for how to shoot and edit song and dance. screenings.title: Some Came Running
screenings.description: Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1958, 137 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Frank Sinatra, Shirley MacLaine, Dean Martin, Martha Hyer, Arthur Kennedy. Minnelli’s phenomenally directed and acted tale of rootlessness in post–World War II America stars Frank Sinatra as a war veteran and former writer who has fallen into alcoholism, and who returns to his Indiana hometown to find nothing is quite as he remembered it. Dean Martin is the unrepentant gambler whom he befriends, and Shirley MacLaine is heartbreaking in a signature early role as a wayward woman who limps after him, hoping he will love her. One of the great American melodramas of the 1950s, this CinemaScope adaptation of James Jones’s novel builds to a frenetic carnival climax that is among Minnelli’s finest achievements. screenings.title: 16mm Cartoons: Raunchy, Sexy & Risqué + Q&A
screenings.description: Back in the ‘pre-code’ era of the 1920s and early 1930s, animated cartoons were made to entertain the adults in the audience. The results were often sexually suggestive, if not borderline explicit. Much later, with the long overdue relaxation of old censorship codes, independent and experimental animators of the 1960s and beyond became free to openly explore the raunchy and risqué once more. Salacious sexiness, lustful adultery, queerness, Peeping Toms, and other questionable—or perfectly human—adult behaviors were only some of the wonderfully ‘vulgar’ themes present in animated shorts made in both eras.

screenings.title: Leave Her to Heaven
screenings.description: A chilling film noir like no other, Gene Tierney stars as Ellen Berent, a beautiful and possessive woman whose overly dependent love for her husband turns increasingly sinister. Shot in gorgeous technicolor by director John M. Stahl and DP Leon Shamroy (winner of the Academy Award for Best Color Cinematography), Leave Her to Heaven became 20th Century Fox’s highest-grossing film of the 1940’s. At the rotten center is an Oscar-nominated performance from Tierney, playing the rare femme fatale who isn’t motivated by all-American greed and ambition, but instead is consumed by obsession, jealousy, and deadly devotion.

screenings.title: Ec: Intolerance
screenings.description: Griffith’s immensely influential silent epic intercuts four parallel tales from history (spanning Babylon, Christ’s Judea, Reformation Europe, and turn-of-the-century America) to embroider a moral tapestry on personal, social, and political repression through the ages. The visual poetry is overwhelming, especially in the massed crowd scenes, and the unbridled eroticism of the Babylon harem scenes demonstrates just what Hollywood lost when it later bowed to the Hays Code. While the (partly self-financed) production ruined Griffith financially and baffled audiences with its multiple plots and labyrinthine structure, it has been enormously influential on generations of filmmakers, including Eisenstein, who studied the film closely.CLICK HERE TO BOOK TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Dr. Strangelove Or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb
screenings.description: Dir. Stanley Kubrick. 1964. 95 mins. 35mm. With Peter Sellers, George C. Scott, Sterling Hayden, Slim Pickens, Keenan Wynn. Stanley Kubrick reinvents the nuclear suspense thriller, then in vogue, as an absurdist black comedy in this brilliant evocation of cold war paranoia. Dr. Strangelove, co-written by Kubrick and Terry Southern, strikes just the right manic, irreverent, sexually charged tone, creating a satirical masterpiece that is one of the seminal counterculture works of the 1960s. Towering over the cast—which also includes George C. Scott as the blustering General Buck Turgidson and Sterling Hayden as “precious bodily fluids”–obsessed General Jack D. Ripper—is Sellers, a triple threat as meek RAF Captain Mandrake, bungling U.S. President Merkin Muffley, and, of course, the mad scientist title character—inventor of the doomsday machine that may wipe out humanity as we know it. screenings.title: The Long, Long Trailer
screenings.description: Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1953, 96 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Lucille Ball, Desi Arnaz, Marjorie Main, Keenan Wynn. Lucy and Desi and Minnelli? Talk about a dream team. In this hilarious mix of romantic comedy, slapstick, and suspense, Ball and Arnaz—at the time the two most popular performers in the nation—play Tacy and Nicky (of course), an engaged couple who purchase a trailer so they can journey the country and play at domesticity before tying the knot. screenings.description: The inimitable Kathleen Collins’s second film tells the story of two remarkable people, married and hurtling toward a crossroads in their lives: Sara Rogers, a Black professor of philosophy, is embarking on an intellectual quest just as her painter husband, Victor, sets off on an exploration of joy. Victor decides to rent a country house away from the city, but the couple’s summer idyll becomes complicated by his involvement with a younger model. One of the very first fictional features by an African-American woman, LOSING GROUND remains a stunning and powerful work of art for being a funny, brilliant, and personal member of indie cinema canon.

screenings.title: Maîtres Anciens – Comédie
screenings.description: “Like Reger – the character [Austrian novelist and playwright] Thomas Bernhard placed on a museum bench facing a painting by Tintoretto, an ‘Old Master’ if ever there was one – an actor finds himself alone and thwarted after a notorious virus forces the indefinite closure of theaters. He wanders through an empty auditorium, paces the now-useless backstage areas, and bursts out into a street haunted by masked passersby. Having persuaded a firefighter to keep watch over him and his explosives, he pours out – to the guard and the surrounding silence alike – his loathing for, among other things, Heideggerians, a lack of punctuality, people who admire rather than respect, and the State’s appropriation of children. At the intersection of cinema and theater, despair and the will to survive, 1980s Austria and 2020s France, Bernhard’s text takes on a new resonance: ‘And as for culture in this country, your stomach exists only to turn.’” –Marie Hermann, FIDMarseillePreceded by:Mathieu Amalric C’EST PRESQUE AU BOUT DU MONDE (2015, 16 min, digital. With Barbara Hannigan.)“In C’EST PRESQUE AU BOUT DU MONDE, I explore a mystery that fascinates me: where do these inhuman voices come from? From where in the body does the unsettling anomaly of singing originate?” –Mathieu AmalricTotal running time: ca. 100 min.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: The Cobweb
screenings.description: Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1955, 134 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Lauren Bacall, Richard Widmark, Gloria Grahame, Lillian Gish, Charles Boyer, John Kerr, Susan Strasberg, Oscar Levant. An essential Minnelli, featuring maybe his most wildly stacked cast, The Cobweb confidently offers up a nearly undefinable mix of the restrained and the truly eccentric. Set in a psychiatric hospital, where the staff is likely more unsettled than the patients, this Cinemascope, Eastmancolor contraption details the fallout after the head doctor’s wife does the unthinkable: she changes the color of the library’s drapes! Long read as a perfect auteur text for Minnelli (who got his start as a window dresser), The Cobweb is a gorgeously shot, low-boil soap opera that’s a must for any 1950s melodrama completist. screenings.title: Ec: Jerome Hill
screenings.description: These 35mm prints are the result of a preservation project undertaken by the Museum of Modern Art.DEATH IN THE FORENOON (1934/66, 2 min, 35mm)CANARIES (1969, 4 min, 35mm)&FILM PORTRAIT(1971, 81 min, 35mm)“FILM PORTRAIT is an autobiography in the sense that it deals explicitly with Jerome’s most personal life’s relationship to film. It draws on film clips taken in his childhood and his whole childhood involvement in art and life. It comes closest to any kind of filmic answer to Proust. […] FILM PORTRAIT is, I believe, the only direct autobiography we have in film. There is Jonas Mekas’s WALDEN, which is diary but not autobiography in a strict sense. We have Cocteau’s BLOOD OF A POET, ORPHEUS, and TESTAMENT OF ORPHEUS. One could say that this last is autobiographical, but it is also allusive and poetic; whereas Jerome’s FILM PORTRAIT is a very straight attempt to present autobiography on film. Of course, subsequently, James Broughton’s TESTAMENT and my own SINCERITY & DUPLICITY series of autobiographical films were very much inspired by Jerome’s FILM PORTRAIT as well as by Jonas’s WALDEN. […] Jerome Hill’s films are great because they are poised on wit and achieve a balance – a gentle, intentional, particularly American balance.” –Stan Brakhage, FILM AT WIT’S ENDTotal running time: ca. 90 min.CLICK HERE TO BOOK TICKETS NOW!

Preserved by the Library of Congress through the Avant-Garde Masters program funded by The Film Foundation and administered by the National Film Preservation Foundation.)A film poem, based on Anaïs Nin’s HOUSE OF INCEST, narrated by and featuring Nin.“[BELLS OF ATLANTIS was] inspired by the prologue to my HOUSE OF INCEST and the line: ‘I remember my first birth in water.’ The film evoked the watery depths of the lost continent of Atlantis. It is a lyrical journey into prenatal memories, the theme of birth and rebirth from the sea.” –Anaïs NinKen JacobsLITTLE STABS AT HAPPINESS (1959-63, 18 min, 16mm. With Jack Smith.)“Material was cut in as it came out of the camera, embarrassing moments intact. 100’ rolls timed well with music on old 78s. I was interested in immediacy, a sense of ease, and an art where suffering was acknowledged but not trivialized with dramatics. Whimsy was our achievement, as well as breaking out of step.” –Ken JacobsHelen Levitt, Janice Loeb, and James AgeeIN THE STREET (1952, 12 min, 16mm, silent. Preserved by Anthology Film Archives.)“Informality is indeed the crucial and virtually definitive quality of IN THE STREET; it is even the guiding principle and vision. […] This is the extreme realization of a classic ‘naturalistic’ genre, the German ‘street film,’ where the street was imaged as the arena of the everyday and random, the channel in which the ‘stream of life’ conveniently became microcosmic.” –Ken Kelman, THE ESSENTIAL CINEMAWillard MaasGEOGRAPHY OF THE BODY (1943, 7 min, 16mm, b&w. Preserved by Anthology with support from The National Film Preservation Foundation.)“The terrors and splendors of the human body as the undiscovered, mysterious continent.” –Willard MaasTotal running time: ca. 55 min.CLICK HERE TO BOOK TICKETS NOW!

screenings.description: Alfred Kralik and Klara Novak are employees at Matuschek and Company, a general store in Budapest. Klara and Alfred are constantly at odds with each other, butting heads and disagreeing on almost everything. screenings.title: Devo: Restorations and Revelations
screenings.description: COLLECTED FILM AND VIDEO WORKS 1976-84PRESENTED BY FILM RESTORATIONIST PETER CONHEIMFormed in the wreckage of the Kent State shootings in 1973, where co-founders Gerald V. Casale and Mark Mothersbaugh were students during the massacre, and still blowing the horn five decades later, Akron’s DEVO would take their subversive pop-art to staggering mainstream success. All the while, they considered themselves to be filmmakers as much as they were a “band.”From their first film onward (1976’s THE BEGINNING WAS THE END: THE TRUTH ABOUT DE-EVOLUTION), they fused their love of Dadaist image-making with their constantly shapeshifting music, confounding their record label by plowing their meager promo budgets into companion films for songs. This program unveils painstaking new restorations and reconstructions of much of this pivotal work (including SATISFACTION, FREEDOM OF CHOICE, WHIP IT, and much more) alongside a host of rarely (and never)-seen live footage, encounters with hapless interviewers, and other spud ephemera, curated specially for Anthology Film Archives by film archivist and musician Peter Conheim (Mono Pause, ex-Negativland, Wet Gate, et al).Total running time: ca. 80 min + discussion and Q&A.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Tár + Live Performance | Instruments of Desire
screenings.description: From writer-producer-director Todd Field comes TÁR, starring Cate Blanchett as Lydia Tár, the celebrated chief conductor of the Berlin Philharmonic. We meet Tár at the height of her career, as she’s preparing both a book launch and a much-anticipated live recording of Mahler’s Fifth Symphony. Over the ensuing weeks, her life and career unravel as allegations of misconduct erode her carefully cultivated public image. The result is a searing examination of artistic authority, institutional politics, and the blurred boundary between mentorship and exploitation.

screenings.title: Minotaur
screenings.description: Intrigue, corruption, betrayal, survival: the walls of the maze are closing in. The latest from Oscar® nominated writer-director Andrey Zvyagintsev (Loveless, Leviathan), Cannes Grand Prix winner MINOTAUR is a twist-laden parable for our times. Russia, 2022. Amidst the comfortable trappings of affluence and domesticity, corporate executive Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov) finds himself under siege on all fronts. At home, he is haunted by suspicions that his increasingly distant wife Galina (Iris Lebedeva) is unfaithful. At work, he contends with a demand from local authorities to draft a quota of employees for the war in Ukraine. Desperate to keep his hands clean, Gleb struggles to reassert control even as the collapse of his carefully ordered life seems fated to accelerate toward violence. A pressure cooker in cinematic form, MINOTAUR uncovers and indicts the heart of societal darkness with searing clarity. Uniting intimately-drawn performances and stark visual power, France’s Best International Feature Film entry to the 99th Academy Awards® is peerless work from an indisputable master.

screenings.title: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall in 35mm
screenings.description: Cameron Winter, in December 2025, after a months-long sold-out tour with his band Geese, returned to New York to play a single show at Carnegie Hall. This is the movie. Directed and shot on 35mm and 16mm by Oscar-winning filmmaker Paul Thomas Anderson (One Battle After Another), the crew includes filmmaker and actor Benny Safdie (The Smashing Machine) and music producer Ariel Rechtshaid (Grammy winner for albums with Vampire Weekend and Adele). GQ praised Cameron Winter’s show at Carnegie Hall as “staggeringly good,” and Nick Cave said he has a "a glorious, emotive voice with brilliant, blistering words, a racked and wondrous thing.” Winter’s solo album Heavy Metal was named one of the best of the year by Pitchfork, Rolling Stone, Paste and Mojo and Geese’s last record Getting Killed was named the best album of 2025 by The New Yorker, NME, and Stereogum.

screenings.title: Xi. Thou Shalt Not Be Indifferent
screenings.description: Mr. Marian Turski, the world-renowned historian, journalist, and until his recent passing, president of the International Auschwitz Committee, takes us back to the roots of evil. A survivor of the Lodz Ghetto, Auschwitz, Buchenwald, and Theresienstadt death camps in his youth, Turski explains with firsthand knowledge and surgical precision how otherwise well-educated and cultured people can, under certain circumstances, turn into criminals and mass murderers. He reminds us about the painful past, explains the present, and warns about the future. His dramatic plea, "do not be indifferent!" remains more relevant now than ever. Andrzej Wolf, the director and cinematographer of this film, pays a loving tribute to one of the last moral compasses of the Greatest Generation.

screenings.title: Lolita
screenings.description: Dir. Stanley Kubrick. 1962. 152 mins. 35mm. With James Mason, Shelley Winters, Peter Sellers, Sue Lyon. “How did they ever make a movie of Lolita?” the savvy, shocked poster tagline wondered. Only Stanley Kubrick would dare try. Outwitting the censors, Kubrick turned Vladimir Nabokov’s 1955 novel about a professor’s obsession with a young “nymphet” into a rich cinematic satire, emphasizing Nabokov’s dark social comedy. A monstrously proper James Mason is unforgettable as Humbert Humbert, whose twisted heart leads him to destroy his own life and soul for the love of the teenage daughter (Sue Lyon) of his crass and lovelorn landlady (Shelley Winters). As the mysterious oddball playwright Clare Quilty, Sellers lends Kubrick’s tragic satire a coherent sense of eccentricity and outlandish humor. screenings.title: Galaxie
screenings.description: A pinnacle of the art of filmic portraiture, Gregory Markopoulos’s GALAXIE comprises thirty short portraits of men and women from across the spectrum of the mid-1960s cultural scene in New York City. Its subjects include many of Markopoulos’s fellow experimental filmmakers – Storm De Hirsch, George & Mike Kuchar, Jonas Mekas, Shirley Clarke, Amy Taubin, and Ed Emshwiller – as well as figures from the literary and art worlds, including Parker Tyler, Jasper Johns, W.H. Auden, Allen Ginsberg, Kenneth Kelman, Maurice Sendak, Susan Sontag, and others. In keeping with Markopoulos’s short-form masterpieces MING GREEN, BLISS, and SORROWS, each of the individual portraits in GALAXIE was edited entirely in-camera, a near-miraculous feat given the intricate use of multiple layers of superimposition, all of it achieved by rewinding and making additional passes through the single 100-foot (ca. 3-minute) roll of 16mm film during the shoot. Initially intending to produce only a handful of portraits, Markopoulos ended up filming 40 different chapters, and ultimately incorporated the first 30 into the completed work (presented in the order they were created). Each of the portraits represents an exquisite visual record of the encounter between subject and filmmaker, while the film as a whole provides an extraordinary opportunity to observe the gradual development of Markopoulos’s approach to portraiture and in-camera editing.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Dinner With Friends + Q&A
screenings.description: After the parties, jobs, and hook-ups throughout their twenties and into their thirties, eight friends are trying to hold on to their group as they get older and life gets complicated. Over a series of dinners, the group deals with loyalty, loss, and an uncertain future as relationships shift and secrets are unraveled, with each dinner bringing its own dynamic shifting announcement of reconciliation, unexpected relationships, and betrayal. The city is crumbling, the climate is changing, and worries about the future of the world are making it hard for this group of friends to stay together. But they’ll come to realize everything would be much harder if they don’t.

Max Turnheim
screenings.description: Few contemporary filmmakers have demonstrated such a sustained commitment to the form of cinematic portraiture as Friedl vom Gröller, whose work is represented throughout this series. While most of her films are notably (and proudly) small in scale, MAX TURNHEIM is an exception, an ever-expanding collection of portraits of a subject she has returned to repeatedly throughout the years.“An allegorical reflection upon physiosocial existence in the world. This to-date 13-part, long-term portrait of Max Turnheim brings the abundance of Friedl vom Gröller’s gaze to complete fruition. The film conceives its portrait through the compression of an entire phase of life, including separation from the parental home, the finding of an individual path, and a renewed longing for middle class institutions. The point of departure for all this content is a face seen over the course of time.” –Alejandro BachmannCLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: The Muppets Take Manhattan
screenings.description: Dir. Frank Oz. U.S., 1984, 94 mins. U.S. DCP. With Jim Henson, Dave Goelz, Jerry Nelson, Richard Hunt, Steve Whitmire, Liza Minnelli. When the Muppets’ college revue is a big hit, they decide to take the show all the way to Broadway. Adjusting to the hustle and bustle of New York City, Kermit takes a job at a local restaurant while he searches for a producer. Filled with cameos by quintessential New Yorkers, such as Gregory Hines, Joan Rivers, James Coco, Brooke Shields, and Liza Minnelli, the movie ends with a fantastical and questionably genuine wedding between Kermit and Miss Piggy. Oz’s first solo-directed film is a dose of pure joy, a true gift to showtune lovers featuring some of the greatest songs in the Muppet canon and the beloved “Muppet Babies” sequence that spawned its own mini-franchise. The latest from Oscar® nominated writer-director Andrey Zvyagintsev (Loveless, Leviathan), Cannes Grand Prix winner MINOTAUR is a twist-laden parable for our times. Russia, 2022. Amidst the comfortable trappings of affluence and domesticity, corporate executive Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov) finds himself under siege on all fronts. At home, he is haunted by suspicions that his increasingly distant wife Galina (Iris Lebedeva) is unfaithful. At work, he contends with a demand from local authorities to draft a quota of employees for the war in Ukraine. Desperate to keep his hands clean, Gleb struggles to reassert control even as the collapse of his carefully ordered life seems fated to accelerate toward violence. A pressure cooker in cinematic form, MINOTAUR uncovers and indicts the heart of societal darkness with searing clarity. Uniting intimately-drawn performances and stark visual power, France’s Best International Feature Film entry to the 99th Academy Awards® is peerless work from an indisputable master.

screenings.title: The Oldest Profession
screenings.description: A meld of ATG and radical pink sensibilities, Noboru Tanaka’s guerrilla-shot apostasy captures its subjects writhing in both agony and pleasure over the course of a sordid Osaka summer.

screenings.title: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall in 35mm
screenings.description: Cameron Winter, in December 2025, after a months-long sold-out tour with his band Geese, returned to New York to play a single show at Carnegie Hall. This is the movie. Directed and shot on 35mm and 16mm by Oscar-winning filmmaker Paul Thomas Anderson (One Battle After Another), the crew includes filmmaker and actor Benny Safdie (The Smashing Machine) and music producer Ariel Rechtshaid (Grammy winner for albums with Vampire Weekend and Adele). GQ praised Cameron Winter’s show at Carnegie Hall as “staggeringly good,” and Nick Cave said he has a "a glorious, emotive voice with brilliant, blistering words, a racked and wondrous thing.” Winter’s solo album Heavy Metal was named one of the best of the year by Pitchfork, Rolling Stone, Paste and Mojo and Geese’s last record Getting Killed was named the best album of 2025 by The New Yorker, NME, and Stereogum.

screenings.title: Xi. Thou Shalt Not Be Indifferent
screenings.description: Mr. Marian Turski, the world-renowned historian, journalist, and until his recent passing, president of the International Auschwitz Committee, takes us back to the roots of evil. A survivor of the Lodz Ghetto, Auschwitz, Buchenwald, and Theresienstadt death camps in his youth, Turski explains with firsthand knowledge and surgical precision how otherwise well-educated and cultured people can, under certain circumstances, turn into criminals and mass murderers. He reminds us about the painful past, explains the present, and warns about the future. His dramatic plea, "do not be indifferent!" remains more relevant now than ever. Andrzej Wolf, the director and cinematographer of this film, pays a loving tribute to one of the last moral compasses of the Greatest Generation.

screenings.title: Knights of Night + Q&A
screenings.description: When a vigilante crew targeting online predators sparks a war with a rival gang that’s a twisted cult, New York City descends into a chaotic fever dream of violence, revenge, and survival.

screenings.title: The Rocky Horror Picture Show (live)
screenings.description: An outrageous assemblage of the most stereotyped science fiction movies, Marvel comics, Frankie Avalon / Annette Funicello outings and rock 'n' roll of every vintage. The madcap musical mayhem begins when rain-soaked Brad and Janet take refuge in the castle of a mad scientist from outer space who is about to unveil his greatest creation - and have a bit of fun with his reluctant guests! Join Tim Curry, Barry Bostwick, Susan Sarandon and rock star Meatloaf in the most popular cult classic of all time.​

screenings.title: Orfeo
screenings.description: In the classic Greek tragedy, a snake bites Eurydice on her wedding day, and her new husband, Orpheus, travels to the Underworld to bring her back. Virgilio Villoresi’s expressionistic adaptation of the tale is based on Dino Buzzati’s 1969 Poema a fumetti, Italy ‘s first graphic novel. The film is a modern reimagining with an aesthetic untethered from reality: a kaleidoscopic journey through time and place, reflecting on art, love, mystery, eroticism, melancholy, life, and death.

screenings.title: Mean Streets + Q&A
screenings.description: Just a Shot Away chronicles the brilliant and tumultuous life and career of Martin Scorsese, one of the world’s foremost living filmmakers, from his childhood on the violent streets of mid-century Little Italy, recreated in unprecedented detail, to his tectonic contributions to the cinema of the New Hollywood and beyond. The making of such masterpieces as Taxi Driver, Raging Bull, and The Last Waltz are explored here in revelatory depth, along with undersung favorites like Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore and After Hours.

screenings.title: Basic Instinct
screenings.description: The brainchild of provocateur extraordinaires Paul Verhoeven and Joe Eszterhas, Basic Instinct was one of the most controversial films of the 90s (protested by LGBT activists for its portrayal of the film’s bisexual femme fatale) and a runaway box office smash. When detective Nick Curran (Michael Douglas) becomes ensnared in a web of sex, lies, and violence, all the evidence points to Catherine Tramell (Sharon Stone, in a star-making role), a seductive, mysterious crime novelist. As the bodies pile up and hidden obsessions are revealed, Curran begins to doubt his investigatory instincts and give in to his baser ones.

screenings.title: Barbara Forever + Q&A
screenings.description: BARBARA FOREVER is an expansive, immersive exploration of the life, work, and ongoing cultural impact of filmmaker Barbara Hammer – a pioneering artist who lived boldly, created urgently, and transformed cinema through her singular vision. Her films were an extension of herself: sensual, experimental, and unapologetically lesbian, rooted in a profound desire for connection and an insistence on telling her own story. Driven by her canon of over eighty films, a vast collection of unreleased archival materials, and extensive audio interviews, Brydie O’Connor’s portrait allows for Hammer’s voice and images to shine through, becoming both a tribute and an extension of her legacy.

screenings.title: Leonora in the Morning Light + Q&A
screenings.description: In the early 1930s, painter Leonora Carrington, a rebel against social expectations, joins the surrealist movement and its iconic figures like André Breton and Salvador Dalí in Paris. A whirlwind love affair with artist Max Ernst confronts her with her inner demons. During the war, Leonora flees to Mexico and finally empowers herself. Today Leonora Carrington is one of the highest selling female painters worldwide, next to Frida Kahlo and Georgia O’Keeffe.

screenings.title: The Scout + Q&A
screenings.description: Sofia works as a location scout for a TV pilot filming in New York City. It’s her job to find the homes, businesses, and exteriors where the show will be filmed. Driving around the city’s different neighborhoods, she enters the private spaces of strangers to photograph their cozy apartments and eclectic shops, stepping into the fabric of their lives while trying to satisfy the demands of her erratic employers. Over a day filled with these encounters, Sofia witnesses moments of curiosity, vulnerability, and quiet tension until her work takes a sudden, personal turn. Drawing from her own experience as a location scout, writer-director Paula González-Nasser captures the poetry and costs of being a young creative. Her celebrated directorial debut The Scout crafts a contemplative exploration of urban disconnection, following one woman’s journey through other people’s worlds as she struggles to find her own.

Love Letter
screenings.description: Pining for a love that is pained and futile, the young mistress of a well-known, married poet spends her days waiting for her lover to return in this subtle, slice-of-life drama made for Roman Porno’s 10th Anniversary. An unusual hit among female spectators.

screenings.title: Angel Guts: Red Classroom
screenings.description: Overwrought with an exuding sense of melancholia in tone and exuberant mise-en-scène, Chusei Sone’s adroitly self-reflexive Red Classroom is a brooding, almost lyrical portrait of Takashi Ishii’s tragic figures of Muraki and Nami, buried in relentless traumas, desires and deep loneliness.

screenings.title: Top Stripper
screenings.description: Directed with remarkable levity, and vibrant, on-location cinematography, Morita’s Top Stripper is an irreverent take on the seishun eiga, raising questions of spectatorship as a young boy falls in love with a dancer. Treating sex as a mere fact of life, Morita captures his subjects' personal lives with heartfelt candor.

screenings.title: Woman on the Night Train
screenings.description: New English Subtitles by Japan Society. A baroque fantasy by way of Vadim and Buñuel’s Diary of a Chambermaid, Noboru Tanaka’s Woman on the Night Train is a gothic work replete with decadent, atmospheric imagery and unravelling psyches.

screenings.title: Scent of a Spell
screenings.description: 2K Restoration. Mermaid Legend director Toshiharu Ikeda’s elegant and spellbinding Scent of a Spell is a moody, psychological tale of a “woman in trouble”, melding eroticism, tragic coincidence and psychological paranoia.

screenings.title: Woods are Wet
screenings.description: An adaptation of Marquis de Sade’s Justine, Tatsumi Kumashiro’s gothic work of depravity follows a young woman who stumbles upon a rural countryside inn governed by sadistic perversions.

screenings.title: Last Cabaret
screenings.description: Focused on a family-run cabaret soon to be shuttered, Shusuke Kaneko’s (Summer Vacation 1999) elegiac Last Cabaret would be the penultimate film in Nikkatsu’s erotic line—a bittersweet requiem for the end of Roman Porno.
